history.content: What is the difference between bulk migration and vMotion?

Bulk migration and vMotion are both methods for migrating virtual machines (VMs) in a VMware environment. Bulk migration is a capability of HCX that uses vSphere replication to migrate disk data while re-creating the VM on the destination vSphere HCX instance. It allows for the migration of multiple VMs concurrently, resulting in more consistent bandwidth use and an overall use of network bandwidth capability higher than a single vMotion. However, individual VMs migrate more slowly with bulk migration, and there is a brief downtime when the new clone VM is brought up on the destination side. Additionally, VMs that depend on disk ordering and disk UUIDs (such as Oracle RAC) can have issues with bulk migration. vMotion, on the other hand, is a VMware feature that allows for the live migration of running VMs from one ESXi host to another without any downtime. It does not change the disk UUIDs on the destination, making it suitable for cluster type applications that require disk UUIDs. However, vMotion migrates only a single VM at a time, and it can generate fluctuations in bandwidth use that would be visible as peaks and valleys within network monitoring tools or the WAN Opt UI.
What are different disk UUIDs and what are they ysed for?

Disk UUIDs, or Universally Unique Identifiers, are unique values assigned to disks in a VMware environment. They are used to identify disks and ensure that the correct disk is associated with the correct VM. When a VM is migrated using vMotion, the disk UUIDs are not changed, which makes vMotion suitable for cluster type applications that require disk UUIDs. However, when a VM is migrated using bulk migration, the disk UUIDs may be changed, which can cause issues for VMs that depend on disk ordering and disk UUIDs, such as Oracle RAC.

IBM Cloud Pak for Data

New beta pitch_percentage query parameter for controlling the global speaking pitch
: The service offers a new pitch_percentage query parameter to modify the speaking pitch for a synthesis request. The speaking pitch represents the tone of the speech that the service synthesizes. It represents how high or low the tone of the voice is perceived by the listener. A higher pitch results in speech that is spoken at a higher tone and is perceived as a higher voice; a lower pitch results in speech that is spoken in a lower tone and is perceived as a lower voice. The parameter changes the per-voice default pitch for an entire request. For more information, see [Modifying the speaking pitch](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/text-to-speech?topic=text-to-speech-synthesis-paramsparams-pitch-percentage).

0.0.0.0/0 is a special case of a CIDR notation, which is allowed. Use it with caution because of the following reasons:



* When you use 0.0.0.0/0 as a block policy, all traffic to and from your Netezza Performance Server database is restricted.
* When you use 0.0.0.0/0as an allow policy, all traffic to and from your Netezza Performance Server database is allowed.



You can use CIDR ranges to represent public and private IP addresses. Devices or services that are in a private or enterprise network that uses private IP addresses have gateways. These gateways typically have network interfaces with public IP addresses, which do network address translation (NAT). This allows entities in the private network to connect to external services.

You must use a CIDR range that represents only the public IP addresses of gateways when you are setting allow and block policies.
